I have not forgotten the measure [of the original] and did not dare to take it all verbatim.
Under each section title, I have followed the thematic divisions established by Master Hanshan;

however, where there were discrepancies, I increased or decreased the content according to my records, ceasing once the essential meaning was conveyed. In instances where certain points were commonly cited by other schools, I have likewise made syntheses and cross-references.
If there are still points that have not been fully clarified, I shall supplement them with my own humble views.

This sutra has traditionally had a great many commentaries. During the Chen and Sui dynasties, there was the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai, who awakened to the *dharmaparyāya-samādhi* and attained the *āvartana-dhāraṇī*.
While residing in Jiangling, he expounded the ten-fascicle *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) as an exegesis of this sutra.

The *Wenju* (Textual Exegesis) consists of ten fascicles as an explanation of the sutra. Reaching the era of the Venerable Jingxi of the Tang dynasty, there appeared the *Shiqian* (Explanatory Sub-commentary) in ten fascicles and the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) in ten fascicles.
Later, during the Yuan dynasty, Master Huigu from Huyaogu composed a commentary based on Tiantai’s *Wenju*.
Subsequently, Master Tianzhu Yijian Ru also followed Tiantai’s tradition, expanding upon the commentary to produce the *Kezhu* (Annotated Outline) in seven fascicles. Regarding these...
Other commentaries are too numerous to list exhaustively; for this present exposition, I take the *Kezhu* (Annotated Outline) as my primary authority.
In truth, it follows the tradition of Tiantai. The essential exegesis cited in this commentary was authored by Master Huan of Wenzhou during the Song dynasty;
the *Zhiyin* (Knowledge of Sounds) was authored by Master Puyu; the *Dakuan* (Great Openings) was authored by Master Yiyun; and the *Zhizhi* (Direct Pointing) was authored by Master Qingqiu.
Regarding the works composed by the Master, I, Xiang, am ashamed that I dwell in a remote and secluded corner, where my learning and experience are meager.
Among the treasures of antiquity and the present day, I cannot help but lament that I have missed nine out of ten.

Regarding the titles established for the sections, although they were originally intended as annotations to the main text, I have excised what was redundant and supplemented what was lacking, desiring in all cases that they accord perfectly with the sūtra.
Thus, regarding the general outline of the "Circulation" section, I have not cited other material at length.
Regarding the sequence of the topical outline (*kē*), I have followed Master Jiāoguāng entirely, employing the sexagenary cycle characters (*gānzhī*) to facilitate easy reference.

However, since each commentary already has its own established structural precedents, it would be inconvenient to record these outlines directly beneath the respective chapters; therefore, I have established this separate topical outline here.

In citing various commentaries below, there are occasional omissions; some passages agree with the original text, while others are interspersed with rare insights or derived from my own ignorant views.
Because these elements are inconsistent, I have not provided specific attributions for them. This is not intended to conceal the merits of others.
Regarding the explanations provided by various masters, whenever the meaning was already clear within the scriptural text itself, I have generally omitted them;

however, for those points that were obscure, I have provided detailed exegesis so that it may be known that the words of the sūtra are inherently neither shallow nor superficial. Wherever the words of ordinary people appear, they are marked with a triangle (△);
where there are citations from other sources, they are distinguished by a circle (○). This is intended to facilitate easy identification for those who consult the text while reading.
Regarding difficult characters in the sutras— whether they follow their original pronunciation or alternative pronunciations—
I have verified each one against character dictionaries so that beginners need not laboriously consult them.

The general purport of the entire sutra is that the Tathāgata’s original intent was for the sake of the one great cause and condition (ekamahā-kṛtya-hetu-pratyaya), to reveal and instruct sentient beings so that those who hear or see it throughout past and present may, from this point on, awaken and enter [the Way]. However, as the text of the sutra is vast and extensive, its beginning and end are difficult to comprehend.
Although it is divided into twenty-eight chapters, if students are not provided with a preliminary overview, they will find it difficult to penetrate [its meaning] in depth.
Therefore, prior to the scripture, I have separately established this "General Meaning" (Dà-yì) to annotate its source.
Since there is a specific charge [to do so], I could not help but proceed. This is not to flaunt my learning or to present my own delusions;
rather, as the various masters have already provided detailed exegeses, how could I be adding superfluous branches outside the main trunk or inventing matters from thin air?
It is truly because the world has declined and the times have deteriorated that people have become increasingly negligent and indolent.

Having grown weary of the vast abundance of the blood, hearts, and marrow of former sages, each person clings to a single corner of knowledge, inevitably harboring partiality. This is why my late father, the Elder, wept with heart-wrenching tears.
Since I am determined to compile this, I, a humble youth, cannot help but exert myself to carry it out.
Regarding the "General Meaning of the Lotus Sutra":
"Wondrous Dharma" (Miaofa) refers to the Ultimate Truth (Paramārtha-satya). Since its meaning is the foremost, there is no other meaning beyond it; truly, it is [inexpressible].

It is that which is named by means of names; yet it cannot be named by means of names. Nevertheless, following the various Sages of antiquity, one must inevitably use this Dharma to instruct and reveal it to those who come after.
Thus, one has no choice but to borrow metaphors to manifest the Dharma, and so it is named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma).
However, this lotus flower also possesses that which is inconceivable; for the Tathāgata expounds the Great [Dharma]...
In the *Avataṃsaka*, at the very beginning, light is emitted from between the eyebrows, bestowing empowerment upon Samantabhadra.
He then enters the Tathāgata-garbha-kāya-samādhi and speaks of the Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean.
Within this ocean is a great lotus named "Various Radiant Filaments and Fragrant Banners. The Flower Treasury Adorned World resides within this lotus. Now, as for this flower...
Within this Flower Treasury Adorned World, there are further infinite and immeasurable varieties of worlds.
Is this Flower Treasury Adorned World conceivable or inconceivable? The Flower Treasury Adornment is inconceivable;
thus one knows all the more that the Lotus is inconceivable. That the Lotus is inconceivable means:
Can the Sublime Dharma be conceived? The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (The Lotus of the Sublime Dharma) establishes its name through mutual metaphor and mutual elucidation;
thus, the name does not obstruct the Dharma, and the Dharma being manifested, the name can be established. To understand this is to grasp the essential purport of the sutra.
However, why is it that the Tathāgata is determined to preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?

It is because our original teacher, Śākyamuni, having assumed a human form and manifested his appearance in the world, originally intended to reveal to all sentient beings this vast Lotus Treasury of the Primordially Endowed, Innate, Perfectly Enlightened, and Wondrously Luminous Mind. Having deliberated and examined this for four [incalculable eons],...

For over ten years, he gradually sought to lead them into the unfathomable ocean of the profound. Yet, he did not expect that those of the five natures and three vehicles would be unable to realize it swiftly.

Therefore, he first preached the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* for them; furthermore, he led them into the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings, where they heard of these immeasurable meanings within the assembly.
Still, they did not recognize that what was vast had been condensed, nor that the root had been revealed and the source made manifest. It was merely...

One attains a painting of empty space, wherein both sound and form are complete in their entirety. Looking upward, the rain of Dharma falls in profusion; looking downward, mountains and rivers roar and crash.

One emits the great radiance from the tuft of hair between the eyebrows, which directly illuminates the eighteen thousand lands of the eastern direction, from Mount Nimiṣa down to the Avīci Hell, leaving nothing unreached.
Within these realms, the appearances of the ten dharma-realms manifest perfectly—both the defiled and the pure.

Joy! Anger! To reveal it all with full sincerity: our World-Honored One has intentionally brought forth all the rare treasures within the Lotus Treasury, placing them upon a single platter, in urgent desire that someone here might accept them. Yet, alas, this entire assembly is cold and indifferent;
there is no one to take them up. Only Ajita likewise feigns ignorance, neither discerning nor responding. How strange, how lamentable!
He was filled with doubt. Surveying the entire assembly, he wondered who might be able to answer him. Casting his gaze about, he beheld Mañjuśrī;
he knew in his heart that this youth had seen many Buddhas in the past and must recognize what is rare. "I shall now question him," he thought.

"Mañjuśrī, the Youth, has intentionally reflected upon the past, and since his vision then accords with what he sees now, his perception of phenomena should be non-dual; I am certain that today’s reality is just as it was."
It is certain that this is identical to the discourse on the Sun, Moon, and Lamp; there is no doubt that it teaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for the sake of instructing bodhisattvas.
Therefore, it says: "I saw the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, whose original light and auspicious signs were like this. By this, we know that the present Buddha intends to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
thus he causes the Tathāgata to emerge from samādhi and praise his virtues, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* proceeds from this.

Thus it is said; the Sūtra author establishes the title based on this. The "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta) generally reveals the phenomena and characteristics of the single true Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), serving as the detailed account of the causes and conditions for the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world for the sake of the one great matter. Among the three divisions [of the sūtra], this constitutes the Introductory Division.

From the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*Upāya-parivarta*) through the eight chapters ending with the "Bestowal of Prophecies upon Learners and Non-learners," these constitute the Main Body of the Teaching regarding the Traces (*śeṣa-mukha*). However...
The single chapter on Expedient Means represents the World-Honored One’s original intent: not relying on verbal explanations, but rather entering meditative concentration and emitting light.
Having intended to refine [beings] for forty years, there must have been those who witnessed the Way in its presence; they attained silent resonance beyond the realm of words.
How could one know that others remain blind, as if facing a wall? Therefore, upon emerging from concentration, he sighed at the virtues of the Buddhas and directly called out, "Śāriputra."
He spoke to Śāriputra, saying: "The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable;
the gateway to that wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter. It is something that no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas can know.
This is like a precipitous cliff on a strange peak or a great torrent of water cascading down, surging and tumbling so that it cannot be stopped or suppressed. This was his praise of the Buddha.
It is an abyss of wisdom that causes one to imagine its state at such a time.
At this moment, all the śrāvakas began to reflect and give rise to doubt, wondering: "Why does the World-Honored One now so earnestly praise the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Buddhas?
Śāriputra, who holds the office of leader and whose wisdom surpasses all others, saw only the front porch and the rear eaves of the hall, and thus harbored doubts.
This is because of the clamor of various arguments. Standing bare-chested before the blade, his integrity and spirit were both stern;

in the presence of others, his majestic virtue was such that he assumed myriad postures, exhausting his strength and voice, saying only this: "From my youth until now, I have never heard of such a Dharma.
Now, the fourfold assembly all harbor doubts. I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound upon this matter. At this, the Tathāgata—
"Let me stop for a moment before speaking; having stopped, I shall speak again—this is precisely the wondrous art of slaying the dragon.

It is like a golden needle that clears away cataracts, reviving the dead and returning them to life. This exposition of the subtle discourse shall cause the assembly to grasp the essential points, thereby clarifying the Buddha-wisdom.

No sooner had he granted permission for questions than five thousand people left their seats and departed. The Buddha, because of this, used it to warn those who have not yet attained realization, and further added:
My diligence in teaching my sons as a Tathāgata may be called earnest, profound, and deep; it is difficult to illustrate and difficult to name.
Hereafter, I shall discuss the causes and conditions for the great matter of transcending the world.

Originally, this was for the purpose of revealing, awakening, and leading all sentient beings into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. I tell Śāriputra: the Buddhas of the ten directions use only one [vehicle].
It is for the sake of the Buddha-vehicle that the Buddha preaches the Dharma for sentient beings; there is no other vehicle, whether two or three.
As for why he speaks of two or three, it is entirely because he had no choice but to do so; these are expedient words.
If my disciples have not heard or known this sutra, they will claim that the Buddhas and Tathāgatas teach and transform only bodhisattvas, while they themselves settle for inferiority.
"This person is not a disciple of the Buddha; they are neither an Arhat nor a Pratyekabuddha. What I have vowed is this:

I desire that all sentient beings be no different from myself. If I were to employ the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) to transform even a single person, I would fall into stinginess and greed; such a thing is impossible for me. Furthermore, it says: 'All Tathāgatas...'"
"By means of immeasurable expedient means, he delivers all sentient beings and causes them to enter the Buddha’s untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
If there are those who hear this Dharma, not one among them shall fail to become a Buddha. Furthermore, it says: "The twelve hundred arhats shall all likewise become Buddhas.
These are all instances where the Tathāgata has emptied his heart and liver, revealing the radiance of his mind, teaching people to believe with earnest sincerity. The Buddha has no dual teachings.
Although the śrāvakas had not yet reached this point, they did not speak aloud; nevertheless, they understood it silently in their hearts.
The Tathāgata, knowing that among his disciples there was faith and understanding, immediately said: "Since you already know this, you have no further doubts.
Their hearts were filled with great joy, for they knew for themselves that they would become buddhas. Thus, Śāriputra saw the flicking of the whip.

The shadowed hooves gallop like the wind; they overturn the narrow bridge and stand upon the ground. Only then does one realize that within the light of the white tuft (ūrṇā-kośa), all things rare and marvelous are beyond doubt.
Thus, the Tathāgata alone attains their full enjoyment, and for the first time, there is a slight degree of entry into the wondrous Lotus Treasury.
According to the ancient judgment, this constitutes the "opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," which is also for the sake of the Tathāgata.
For those of superior faculties, the entanglements of the formal exposition have been fully revealed through one complete cycle of teaching.

Since there has been both explanation and demonstration, the Tathāgata has likewise used these as a means to lead them into the Buddha-wisdom, enabling them to suddenly perceive the true reality through the gate of skillful means.
This is precisely the reason for the "opening of the provisional and revealing of the real," and thus it constitutes the "Expedient Means" chapter. [End of] Chapter.
Since Śāriputra’s wisdom was already twice that of others and his learning was no shallow matter, he relied upon his resolute mind and iron-like backbone to shoulder this responsibility.
He was thus able to repent and reproach himself; with grief and joy arising together within him, he said:
"From the past until now, throughout day and night, I have constantly reproached myself. Yet today, from the Buddha, I have heard the never-before-heard and unprecedented Dharma, which severs..."
All doubts and regrets vanished; his body and mind became serene, and he attained a sense of swift peace and security.

Only today does he know that he is born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by the Dharma, and has obtained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma. Contemplating the meaning of these words, Śāriputra was like one awakened from a nightmare, with a sense of joy and relief pervading his entire being.
Indeed, there was not even a hair’s breadth of doubt remaining, which is why it is said he was "serene" and "at peace."
The Recluse has truly reached the ground of non-doubt; therefore, he dares to speak freely, claiming his share of the Buddha-Dharma.

This alone is sufficient to speak of the Great. It is for this reason that the Tathāgata, before the assembly of devas and humans, is finally able to set his mind at ease and cast off all apprehension.
To fill the mouth with words: for twenty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, I have constantly taught and transformed you;

you, too, have constantly followed me through the night to receive instruction. Since we have thus constantly taught and constantly followed one another, how could Śāriputra and the Buddha ever have been separated for even a moment?
Since they were never separated for even a moment, the forty years during which he was muddled and confused cannot be said to have been entirely without foundation.

Therefore, it is because the Great Teaching’s manifestation must have its proper time. When the time arrives, one gains self-confidence; through confidence, one reaches certainty, and thus the teaching is established.
Hence it is said: "Now, for your sakes, I shall speak of the most ultimate reality. This was precisely the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) upon Śāriputra.
From this day forward, until the future attainment of Buddhahood, regarding the primary and secondary adornments (*sambhoga-kāya* and *nirmāṇa-kāya*) and the turning of the wheel [of Dharma]...

Next, he bestowed the prophecy. There was the Bodhisattva Sthiramati. However, from the time of Śāriputra downward, all the śrāvakas had long been stalled in the provisional vehicle and had not yet attained swift realization. Upon seeing that Śāriputra had personally received the prophecy, they immediately gave rise to the Great Mind;
each one removed the upper robe they were wearing to offer as an act of worship to the Buddha, precisely to manifest this.
He attained this by first resolving his mind upon liberation from suffering. Śāriputra, seizing the opportunity, requested further instruction, saying:
"I am now free from all doubt and regret; I have personally received this prediction of future enlightenment before the Buddha.

However, these twelve hundred people have not yet completed their journey on the Noble Vehicle and cannot escape the heavy net of doubt. By what means may they cast off these manifold doubts and achieve the wondrous [state]?"

[The Bodhisattva] attained awakening. Thereupon, the Tathāgata had no choice but to shift his register and change his melody, singing a folk song once more to provide an analogy and recount the preceding events.
He declared that there is no peace within the three realms; they are as manifest as a great burning house.
Yet the children play and take delight therein, disbelieving my words and failing to recognize me as their father, heedlessly running hither and thither.
He played about, utterly devoid of any sense of fear. When the elder saw the fire rising from all four sides, his expression was one of urgent distress and panic beyond measure.
Although the father employed a thousand means to rescue him, the son remained obstinate and ignorant, his tears soaking his long robe until they nearly flowed down in streams.
By chance, he devised a plan and provided three chariots, which seemed acceptable.
Taking advantage of what his sons previously desired, he exhorted them, saying: "O my children, I have described many hardships;
you should all come out quickly. I have prepared three chariots for you, which are now outside the gate, where you may play.
If you do not take them now, you will surely fall into grief and regret. Thinking thus, they rushed toward what they liked, as if leaping over ten thousand deaths at once.

Having escaped the burning house, my anxious thoughts have found some rest; yet I do not realize that my weariness and stubbornness remain firmly rooted, and my dull stagnation is difficult to dispel.
Though I have managed to sit at the crossroads, I still languish in drunken attachment to the thatched hut. Just as I am about to leave the fire, I am once again drowning in a deep abyss.

How painful is this paternal heart! How could it be set aside? Thus, the sons feared that their father would reveal [the truth] without providing recompense, which gave rise to their desire to request the carts.

However, one must understand the reason for requesting the carts: it was because they saw that the sons had attained great enlightenment, having previously lived in delusion within the burning house, while believing the three carts outside the gate to be real. Today, they have attained the realization of the Way.
Kumārajīva: [The father] recognized that his son’s mind was merely a provisional construction; he knew it was fundamentally non-existent yet intentionally sought it out.
Thus, there was a meeting of the minds between father and son. Therefore it is said: "We pray you grant us the three kinds of precious chariots as previously promised.

Because the elder [son] thus requested and obtained the fulfillment of his private desire, the father bestowed upon him chariots equal to those of his other sons, granting them equally without distinction. As for that...
He bestowed upon him a carriage, adorned with various precious gems and further provided with a crimson pillow; it was drawn by white oxen and attended by servants and concubines.
His heart of love and compassion can be called ultimate, and his method of providing for him can be called perfect.
How could one say that the father’s heart was not universal, but instead bestowed its joy only upon someone in particular? Furthermore, how could one say he merely permitted the old [custom]?
Is it equitable or inequitable? Having already provided this analogy, I shall next clarify my discourse: "The three realms of existence here are all mine;
the sentient beings therein are all my children. My love is without partiality, and I do not allow any single person to attain nirvāṇa alone.
If you can believe and accept these words, then all of you shall surely attain it."
To attain the Buddha-way is the foremost vehicle; it is pure and subtle. By mounting this precious vehicle, one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
This is precisely like the Tathāgata raising his oars and stirring the waves, providing the means for those on the same boat to reach the shore. Furthermore, he said:
"I have proclaimed this Dharma-seal for the sake of benefiting the world. Wherever you travel, do not propagate it recklessly. Thus it concludes.
This illustrates that the merit of one who upholds [the teaching] surpasses all else, such that their blessings cannot be compared;
likewise, the transgression of one who destroys it is beyond words. It is as if the Tathāgata were a thunderclap resounding through the vast sky:

when people, like withered trees, encounter the rain, they clearly perceive the sincerity of the father’s intent, and the son’s mind understands it fully without exception. All of this is understood through metaphor; therefore—
This chapter is titled "The Parable. From this point onward, these great disciples, through a single parable, come to feel the Buddha’s compassionate grace.

They first perceive that whether grasping a rabbit or grasping an elephant, the exertion applied is entirely equal. Having recognized that the Buddha’s kindness is difficult to repay, they first feel ashamed of their own dullness and lack of cultivation.
Thus, before the Buddha, they present their faith and understanding through skillful parables: like a destitute son who is content to remove filth.
Within the "Gate of Vermilion," there are subtle and winding critiques that are no less thorough and clear than the Tathāgata’s description of the burning house.
In describing the elder’s extreme and pitiable paternal concern, he captures the true state of affairs;

in depicting the impoverished son’s stubborn ignorance and lack of insight, he provides a most poignant realization. One thus recognizes the hidden resonance between the "knocking" and "singing" of this single assembly on Vulture Peak.

Performing with winding movements and a plaintive clarity, where sorrow and joy arrive in alternation, he manifests as a stage play of myriad forms and ten thousand states—the true reality of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world and the true realm of the Bodhisattvas’ supportive transformation.
He exhausts all that was previously taught and realized over forty years, yet leaves no trace behind. Finally, he says: "The great wealthy elder..."
"This is the Tathāgata. We are all like sons of the Buddha; because we formerly delighted in the Lesser Dharma, the Tathāgata allowed us to be neglected.
Had we possessed a mind that delighted in the Great [Dharma], the Buddha would have preached the Mahāyāna for us.
Now, in this sutra, he speaks only of the One Vehicle, wherein all shall become Buddhas. Therefore, we say that originally our minds did not exist."
That which we had long sought—the great treasure of the Dharma King—has now arrived spontaneously.
We are now true Arhats, worthy of receiving offerings from all among gods and humans. All such things are due to the power of parables;
having fully realized the Buddha’s mind, how can the grace of this hidden benefit be sufficiently described? If one were to wish to repay this heart and this virtue, even with one's hands...
Even if one were to provide for them, prostrate at their feet, and pay them homage for immeasurable eons, one could not repay their kindness;
nor could one do so by carrying them on one's two shoulders for more than as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges;
nor even by offering immeasurable precious robes, various medicinal decoctions, or even ox-head sandalwood to construct stupas and temples—none of these can repay it. Even if one were to perish...
How could one possibly repay even a ten-thousandth part of such profound kindness with this life, which is but ashes and form?

Observing the manner in which Kāśyapa and others sought to repay their debt of gratitude, their words and intentions were so poignant that one first realizes their understanding must have been deep and their faith manifoldly earnest; thus they came to awaken to the Tathāgata.
The various teachings are fundamentally intended for entry into this One Vehicle, so that they may utilize provisional means to accord with the ultimate reality;

therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding. Today, the World-Honored One knows that all the śrāvakas have already attained faith and understanding, yet fearing that their faith and understanding might not be profound, he further expounds the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs, so that they may know how the single rain moistens the three types of grasses and two types of trees, each according to its kind.
This shall increase. Furthermore, for the sake of those of the two vehicles, in order to fulfill their profound faith, it was said:

"Kāśyapa has well spoken of the Tathāgata’s true merits; it is indeed as you have said. Yet the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits, which you could not exhaustively describe even in immeasurable billions of kalpas. The appearance of the Tathāgata in the world is like..."
A great cloud arose, and with a vast sound, it proclaimed everywhere to all beings: "May those who have not crossed over be enabled to cross;
may those who are not at peace find peace; may those who have not attained nirvāṇa attain nirvāṇa; and may all reach the ground of omniscience. It further says:
"What you all practice is the path of the bodhisattva; by gradually training and studying, you shall all attain buddhahood.

From this, it is known that the Tathāgata’s original teaching is solely the One Vehicle (ekayāna), without a second or a third. The reason for the distinctions among them is due to the differences in the capacities of sentient beings.
When the assembly heard this, their attachments and views were suddenly eliminated, and they first entered the wisdom of the Dharma of equality. Therefore, following this—

There is a chapter on the bestowal of prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*). Although four types of prophecy are enumerated, the actual intention was to bestow the prophecy upon the five hundred [monks] immediately;
however, because the distant causes had not yet manifested, there was concern that they might find it difficult to believe suddenly. Therefore, he first declared:
"My disciples, endowed with majestic power, numbering five hundred, shall all receive their prophecies; in a future age, they shall all attain [Buddhahood]."
The Buddha. Thus, the compiler of the sutra has designated this chapter with the title "Bestowal of Prophecies" (*Vyākaraṇa*).

Up to this point constitutes the first cycle of the Parable Teaching, wherein the prophecies were bestowed upon those of medium capacity. Next is the second cycle, the Teaching on Causes and Conditions (*Nidāna*), for those of inferior capacity;
following the remainder of these prophecies, it says: "I and you all—our past-life causes and conditions I shall now explain. You all..."
Listen well. Hereafter, the Parable of the Phantom City is expounded. Now, why does the Tathāgata necessarily wish to explain the causes and conditions?
It is because, after Śāriputra attained understanding through the discourse on the Dharma, he conceived a longing for the Great Vehicle and said, "Today we are truly the sons of the Buddha.
This was his conviction, free from doubt; therefore, the Tathāgata must respond accordingly.
It is fitting that he bestows this prediction upon them. The four great disciples have now expressed their realization and understanding, saying:
"We who were previously considered true Arhats only now realize that our former title of 'Arhat' was entirely devoid of substance.
This may be called the realization of the mind’s characteristics and essential nature; that he grants them this prediction is likewise most appropriate. Had they been without such aspiration...
With a great mind, he forcibly ceded the precious throne to him. This is like playing the Nine Shao melodies to entertain a sacred magpie upon the temple hall;
not only does its food become uneasy for it to peck at, but it further becomes dazed by desire until death.
For this reason, he must necessarily act as one of inferior capacity and recount the causes and conditions. Precisely when he was expounding these causes and conditions, he raised [the example of]...
The Buddha is called "Greatly Penetrating Wisdom" (Mahābhijñājñāna), and his time is called "Dust-Point Kalpas" (Rajopama-kalpa).
Yet, that the kalpas of dust and the Buddha of wisdom are coextensive from beginning to end is due to the nature of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Within this, the account of the Buddha of Wisdom’s beginning and end is exhaustive in its detail and brevity; the description of the Prince’s cultivation of practice is thorough in its sincerity. This extends even to that Buddha...
Having accepted the invitation, he first turned the Wheel of Dharma three times; as a śrāmaṇera, he further preached the teachings and delivered beings across the sands of the Ganges.
Listening to his words, they seemed as if they could be sought at every step; yet when one reflects upon the matters themselves, their true intent is difficult to fathom.

It is like a recluse listening for the sound of autumn in the dead of night: the more one hears, the more it fades into mystery; the further one pursues it, the more it reveals its reality. It seems real, yet...

It is empty, like a thread, like something fragile; there is a certain indistinct yet profound sentiment that cannot be grasped or imitated, existing only within the space between the mind and the eyes—it can be imagined only by the reclusive sage.
Below this, it is as if the sound of a bell that has already ceased is suddenly taken up again, whereupon it says:
"Those sixteen śrāmaṇeras have all now become Buddhas; the sixteenth was none other than I, Śākyamuni."

In the Sahā world, he attained Buddhahood. O bhikṣus, those immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, whom I converted when I was a śrāmaṇera, are none other than you bhikṣus here, as well as the śrāvaka disciples who will appear in future ages after my parinirvāṇa. As previously stated, they are like the thousand...
The waves surge in competition, all recounting events from kalpas before the dust settled; yet upon reaching this point, a single phrase cuts them off entirely.

It is much like being within a green cloth curtain, when suddenly, from outside the main text, a single move is extracted, leaving one unable to find its point of origin no matter how hard one searches.
This is then followed by the metaphor of the conjured city (*nirmita-pura*), as it is said: "For example, five hundred *yojanas*..."
There was a perilous and difficult path where many people wished to travel to reach a place of precious treasures.
At that time, there was a guide who led them forward until they had already traveled three hundred *yojanas*. Then, they conceived the desire to turn back.

Seeing their plight with compassion, the guide used his power of wisdom to manifest a transformation city, enabling them to rest and recover so that they might obtain the treasures and return home. And...
All the travelers, while at the conjured city, immediately conceived the thought that it was secure;
they never considered for what purpose their original journey began, nor what they had originally sought.

When the Guide knew that their fatigue had ceased but they still clung to this unreal city, he suddenly extinguished the conjured city and clearly revealed the place of treasure, instructing them, saying: "Treasure..."
The destination is near; this city is not real, but is merely a transformation created by me as a place of rest.

Only when the traveler first realizes that the place of attachment is not true will they, before their journey is finished, again each sharpen their former resolve and pray to return to the precious abode.
At the end, it is concluded: "The Teacher of all Buddhas, for the sake of rest, spoke of nirvāṇa. Once it is known that this is but a rest, [he] leads [them on]."
Because they were entering the Buddha’s wisdom, Pūrṇa and all the other śrāvakas rose from their seats, bowed their heads at his feet in prostration, and withdrew to stand to one side;
they gazed up at the Tathāgata with unblinking eyes, doing nothing else.
At that moment, the Tathāgata bestowed upon them a prophecy of enlightenment, like offering water to one who is parched with thirst—how could it fail to reach the very core of their being?
As for the source of transmission and reception, it is cool and refreshing; there is not one instance in ten thousand where error occurs. Because of this, Pūrṇa reflected:
"I know that the World-Honored One is extraordinary and rare, conforming to the various dispositions of the world and uprooting sentient beings from their attachments everywhere.
Regarding the Buddha’s merits, we cannot express them in words; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can truly know them."
This was our profound aspiration from the depths of our hearts. Because the Tathāgata turned his attention toward us, he was able to announce it clearly to the great assembly, saying:
"Do you see this Pūrṇa? I have always declared him to be the foremost among those who preach the Dharma;
therefore, after bestowing the prediction of enlightenment upon Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, I have further bestowed predictions upon all the śrāvakas, saying that they shall all likewise [attain it]."
Because their predictions were given identically as "Universal Radiance" (Puming), there is the "Chapter on the Prediction for the Five Hundred Disciples.
Now, although Ānanda and Rāhula were the Tathāgata’s own close kinsmen, they instead received their predictions after all the others;

this was done, firstly, to encompass those still in training (śaikṣa), and secondly, to demonstrate that there is no distinction between near and distant, showing that the compassionate grace of the world-transcending one is equal and non-dual.

How could there be anyone who distances those who are distant and draws near those who are already near? It is for this reason that the category of "Bestowal of Prophecy upon Learners and Non-learners" exists.
In the "Dharma Master" chapter, the Tathāgata bestows a broad prophecy regarding this life and future lives;
therefore, through the medium of Bhaiṣajyarāja, he informs the eighty thousand great beings so that they may know they are destined to attain Buddhahood.
"O person, it is precisely this and that which I mean when I say: 'I see within this great assembly those of the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings who seek the Buddha-way.

If they now hear even a single phrase or a single verse of this sutra, or even for a single moment feel sympathetic joy, I shall bestow upon them all the prediction of their attainment of Buddhahood. This extends even to after my parinirvāṇa; if there should be anyone who..."
"Whoever hears even a single phrase or a single verse of this sutra and rejoices in it for even a single moment, I shall likewise bestow upon them the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is the universal mind and universal vow of the World-Honored One; through the cause of realization (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*), he pledges his will to deliver infinite beings.
Furthermore, it is essential that all those present in this assembly personally enter the wondrous Lotus Treasury and offer praise."
The merit of those who uphold, recite, and transcribe this sutra, as well as the demerit of those who believe in it or disparage it, are both extraordinary and beyond compare.

Therefore, it is said that just as one who exerts effort in digging a well will easily find water after a long time, it is essential for people to know that by upholding and expounding this sutra, the attainment of Buddhahood is not far off. This is intended to make them realize the Lotus Treasury Ocean.
This marks the departure from the current location. The nine chapters above were traditionally judged by the ancients to be the "Opening of the Buddha’s Knowledge and Vision.

Thus, the Tathāgata’s original intent for appearing in the world is largely fulfilled, and his anxious concern is somewhat relieved; this constitutes the propagation of the *Ji-men* (Trace Gate). However, it does not end here;
there remain four further chapters below, all of which also constitute the propagation of the *Ji-men*. One beholds the Tathāgata...

In this sutra, the exhortation is most earnest. Previously, for the sake of others, it was explained clearly and in detail so that they might believe and know that each person possesses these flowers as the very root of attaining Buddhahood;
yet, this was still a manifestation through words while the signs themselves were not yet fully revealed.
Therefore, a jeweled stūpa five hundred yojanas high emerged from the earth, and the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna appeared in its entirety.
Remaining in this body so that all who see or hear him would not be confused, Mahāpratibhāna acted according to the needs of the occasion.

Desiring to open this stūpa, the Tathāgata showed him that because that Buddha had made a profound and solemn vow, it must wait for his emanation-buddhas to assemble at that gathering before it could be opened. Thereupon, the World-Honored One emitted light to summon the three [assemblies].
The Sahā world was transformed; its realm was such that it could not even be conceived by thought.

At this moment, not only were the Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the present seen dwelling together within the precious stupa, but one also beheld immeasurable emanation Tathāgatas, their forms diverse and their ranks arrayed like shadows, their radiant colors scattering like shooting stars.
It was as solemn as a ten-thousand-acre expanse of clear sky, where the myriad stars shine with brilliant clarity.
The radiance shines from the lair of the moon-frog; its light extends so far, its realm is so vast, the Buddhas are so numerous, and the flowers are so wide.
It is as if a magnificent ink painting of the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu) had been completed in a single scroll.
Within the eyebrows and eyelashes of all people, are these not the manifest medicinal incense banners and flowers, unfolding and multiplying without end? Since the true realm is thus...
“Luo (Lu)! True wisdom shall now arise. The Tathāgata, by means of his supernormal powers, has brought the great assembly together to dwell in the void.
With a great voice, he proclaims to the fourfold assembly: ‘Who among you is able to extensively expound this sutra?
Now is precisely the right time. Before long, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa. I wish to entrust this wondrous Lotus Sutra to you.’”

There is a reason for this. Previously, because those of the various Hīnayāna vehicles had given rise to the vast and great mind, they were immediately granted predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
That this sutra is now entrusted to them is intended to encourage them to practice the vast and great conduct. Furthermore, it says:

"Although the Holy Lord, the World-Honored One, has long since entered parinirvāṇa, he still comes for the sake of the Dharma while remaining within the jeweled stupa; why then do you people not strive diligently for the sake of the Dharma?"
This is an exhortation for the śrāvakas to practice the Great Dharma. Now, as for the title "The Chapter on the Jeweled Stūpa," the emphasis lies in the intimacy of hearing and seeing [the Buddha].
The ancient masters judged this to be a demonstration of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; the meaning of this is extremely clear.
I, too, consider it to be a manifestation of the single, true, wondrous realm, serving as the text for the Tathāgata’s call for its circulation. The World-Honored One...
This was a bitter and earnest exhortation, yet not a single person emerged from the assembly to take it upon themselves.
Furthermore, I spoke of how in the past, when he was Devadatta, he diligently sought the sublime Dharma, not sparing even his own body or life;
this is why today he has become the Unsurpassed One who universally delivers all sentient beings, for in those causal conditions he possessed a vast mind and practiced with diligent effort.

They relinquish their heads, eyes, marrow, and brains without any sense of weariness or attachment. Once you have received your prediction of enlightenment, you may think that attaining Buddhahood is merely your original state and ask, "Why must I labor so hard to practice in this way?

But do you not reflect that although the principle is realized suddenly, its realization depends on the gradual removal of obstacles? If you do not apply yourself to cultivation, even if you were to attain Buddhahood, it would be nothing more than a bare Dharma-body.
If one aspires to the adornment of the myriad virtues and the full accomplishment of the powers and fearlessnesses, is this not difficult?
Alas, for the Tathāgata to teach the śrāvakas is an exceedingly difficult matter. To speak of it as easy would lead them to slacken their cultivation;
to speak of it as difficult would cause them to abandon their great resolve. Therefore, he now raises the difficulty of practice and maintenance in order to spur them on.
Before her illness had ended, a dragon girl who was only eight years old attained Buddhahood in an instant;
this may be called "a mere snap of the fingers," whereby she suddenly transcended to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Thus, one sees that it is extremely easy and not difficult.
Yet, wishing to harmonize the perspectives of the two vehicles so they may understand that this Dharma lies between the easy and the difficult, one must simply not harbor a deliberate mind.
It can be attained; yet, one must not seek it with a mind devoid of intent. Nevertheless, there is something further to be said regarding this:
the Tathāgata is like a merchant in a marketplace who displays hundreds of wonders and thousands of marvels to the people.
This is nothing other than a desire to achieve self-satisfaction while benefiting others; it is not merely to dazzle the eyes of men. As for that dragon’s anger—
Moreover, it is poisonous; yet the female organ is the most supple, such that it may be called the ultimate in being difficult to transform.
Even so, upon hearing this sutra once, their ordinary passions are instantly reformed. How much more so for human beings, and how much more so for those among humans who possess wisdom?

At that time, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Mahāpratibhāna saw that the assembly was filled with men of exceptional talent, all of whom were concealing their capacities and biding their time, unable to exert their vigor and strength.
They specifically stood before the Buddha, made a vow, and expressed their inner thoughts, encouraging and consoling the Tathāgata, saying:
"May you have no anxiety; in future ages, we shall uphold and expound [this teaching] without begrudging our own bodies or lives."
This sutra serves as the guiding cause for this assembly, enabling each member to make vows to bring joy and consolation to the Tathāgata.
Yet, one who draws a crossbow bolt weighing a thousand *jin* does so with a specific purpose in mind;
likewise, the actions of Bhaiṣajyarāja and others as they braved the waves and gales were likewise undertaken with a specific intent. Thus, the five hundred arhats—suddenly...
With profound sincerity, eight thousand students rose from their seats in unison.

Although they did not dare to recite [the scriptures] in this turbid Sahā world, they were nonetheless capable of upholding them within this distracted land. Among the bhikṣuṇīs was Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, my maternal aunt;
though her resolve was set upon presiding over the propagation of the sutras, she suffered from the lack of the Buddha’s own personal authorization.
[The Buddha] recorded it. Before he had even uttered the words he wished to speak, the Tathāgata had already observed his countenance and grasped this intention.
Therefore, he said: "Did you think in your heart that I would bestow a prediction of enlightenment upon you without mentioning your name? I have already spoken of you in general terms."
All the śrāvakas have already received their predictions. Now, if you wish to know your own prediction:

you shall serve as a great Dharma teacher in the presence of sixty-eight thousand *koṭis* of buddhas, and thereafter you will attain buddhahood under the name Sarvasattvapriyadarśana (He Who Is Seen with Joy by All Sentient Beings).
Thereupon Yaśodharā also received her prophecy; thus, it was indeed fitting that the community of nuns should propagate this sutra.

Furthermore, when the Buddha prophesied that his maternal aunt would surely become a great Dharma Master for ten million kalpas, he did so out of concern that the wisdom of the nuns might not keep pace with their merit, wishing instead to have them extensively cultivate the monastic discipline so that they might benefit themselves and others. If this is so—
Thus, the guidance provided by the Medicine King and others may be described as "a single drop completing the whole vessel. How shallow their merit would be!

Although the Śrāvakas have all advanced, one fears they will find it difficult to remain complete while engaging with the mundane world. It is essential that the Bodhisattvas assist them at their side;
this, moreover, is the profound intention of the Tathāgata’s mouth—what he desires to say but cannot express. One must simply look toward...
There were only eight hundred trillion bodhisattvas. Furthermore, these great beings also knew that the Buddha’s mind made no distinctions;
their aspiration lay in protecting the practice. Thereupon, before the Buddha, they let out a lion’s roar and said:

"We shall enable sentient beings to receive, uphold, read, and recite [this teaching], to practice according to the instructions, to attain right mindfulness, and to reach it in this terrifying and evil world."
Among them, there were certain ignorant people who reviled me with foul language and even attacked me with swords and staves.
We, out of reverence and faith in the Buddha, endured these various hardships. We did not cherish our own bodies or lives, but only valued the unsurpassed Way.

It should be known that these bodhisattvas—both their forms and their speech—were originally śrāvakas for whom [the Buddha] had made a prediction; they were depicted as models to serve as examples. This...
Seeing this father and son, one realizes that there is no difference between founding a dynasty and maintaining its success;
thus, this chapter is titled simply with the single character "upholding" (持). Next, the practice of peaceful bliss is explained; this is Mañjuśrī’s specific insight.

His intention was that rather than making it difficult to propagate the sutra through enduring hardships, it would be better to do so without difficulty; therefore, he requested the Tathāgata [to teach this].
He set forth four practices as a means to avoid harm. He taught that one must first perfect oneself and only then seek to perfect others;
he has never seen a case where one has perfected themselves yet others do not follow.

If one can truly purify oneself and exhaust sincerity, being loyal, trustworthy, sincere, and respectful, then even in the lands of the barbarians, I can practice these teachings. Now, among these four practices...

By adhering to the proper spheres of conduct and immediate surroundings, and by being dedicated to the nature of precepts, one may distance oneself from reproach and remain untainted by the various difficulties.

With a profound mind, one does not offend others; with a compassionate mind, one does not abandon the multitude. When these four practices are perfected, one’s regulation of things becomes solemn and majestic.
Yet, attributing this merit to the wondrous Lotus Treasury is not in vain. This is illustrated by the single metaphor of the jewel in the topknot.
It reveals the foremost merit and proclaims the wondrous Lotus Sūtra, ultimately accomplishing all-encompassing wisdom (sarvākārajñatā) and perpetuating the ancestral legacy for a thousand autumns;
nothing exceeds this. As for the circulation of its practice, more than half has already been considered.

Having fully explained the intent of "opening the provisional to reveal the real," the following section further elucidates the "traces" to reveal the "source," which is likewise divided into the introduction and the main body.
Circulation: The first half-fascicle, which emerges from the earth, serves as the introductory section (nidāna) until you yourselves shall hear it through the unfolding of events.
That which emerges from the earth is solely the principle of the venerable one’s own inherent nature;

whereas the various chapters previously discussed in the Trace Gate (jimon) were all matters of phenomenal appearance, here in this Fundamental Gate (honmon), the scope of the objective realm within the light described in the Introductory Chapter is once again completed.
Consequently, there were bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of eight Ganges Rivers who came from other directions, each vowing to extensively preach this sutra here in this Sahā world.
The World-Honored One turned his head away and paid them no heed, intending to show that these were not his own family treasures;

he hoped instead for something to flow forth from his own breast, capable of covering both heaven and earth. Therefore, he said: "I myself have bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers..."
"Sa. He was able to penetrate this sutra. Before his discourse had even concluded, the earth throughout the three thousandfold world-system immediately quaked and split open.

Immeasurable Bodhisattvas surged forth from within the earth. This truly symbolizes that within the Lotus Treasury of every person, there are inherently immeasurable inherent virtues that adorn this place;
it is also like a single scroll of the Eight Arrayed Battle Formations, where one sees only the stars.
The pieces are spread out like a chessboard, and the principal and attendant figures stand in dense array.
Within the Great Hero’s tent, though he does not personally issue commands to the three armies, his strategic calculations have already been settled within the central command’s brocade curtains.

Among the countless people in the assembly, they merely listen to the sounds of horns and gongs, unaware that they have already crossed the Chen-cang Pass. Ajita could not bear to sit idly by and watch this come to pass.

Defeated, he held his spear across his shoulder to face the vanguard; having fathomed the hearts of the army and secretly understood their subtle strategies, he spoke a verse to request an inquiry, saying:
"O immeasurable thousands of myriads of kotis, great assembly of Bodhisattvas, such as have never been seen before—may the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings speak, and so forth.
This question was precisely Maitreya’s desire to exhale for the Tathāgata and bring forth his far-reaching [intent].
In the beginning, before answering, the Buddha merely exhorted them, saying: "You should all with one mind don the armor of diligence and resolve upon a firm will.
This is like desiring to be brave and sharp when facing an enemy; one must first strike at the vital core to achieve success and only then cease.
When he said, "That which I now reveal for you is the wisdom of all Buddhas," this is the wisdom of all Buddhas themselves.

Regarding the power of supernormal faculties, the power of the lions’ springing leap of all Buddhas, and the power of the fierce and great majesty of all Buddhas—one must be able to perceive their emblems. On the surface of the title, there is already a section that devours Qin and devours Chu.
His ambition is as vast as if there were no heavens above and as dense as if there were no earth below; yet the divine workings within it can be fully understood.
How could such a thing be reached by the knowledge and vision of the *śrāvaka* stage (*jīkmun*)? Therefore, I have appended this [chapter], the "Chapter on the Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*).
Suppose there were five hundred thousand million billion nayuta asaṃkhyeya worlds... and so forth.

Suppose a person were to grind all these worlds into fine dust. Starting from the east, they would pass through five hundred thousand million billion nayuta asaṃkhyeya worlds and drop a single grain of dust.
Continuing in this manner until all the dust has been exhausted, [they would mark] all those worlds previously consisting of such fine dust.

All are ground into fine dust. If one were to take all these particles as a measure for my lifespan, it would still exceed this by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayuta-asamkhyeya* kalpas.

Because these particles have an end, while the kalpas of my lifespan are inexhaustible—vast and boundless, its intent and expression are inconceivable; one looks upward with nothing to grasp and drills downward with nothing to enter.
Is this not indeed the power of the Buddhas' sovereign supernormal penetrations, their great might, and their fierce majesty?

Having heard that the Tathāgata’s lifespan is thus, the question previously asked—“From whom did you first resolve to attain enlightenment?”—is answered by the Bodhisattva Earth-Treasury (Dharaṇīśvara) without the need for further explanation.
What more, then, is there to doubt? From the section on Sadāprarudita up to this fifth chapter.

It is also clear that the ancient judgment [of this teaching] as the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is correct. At this time, the great assembly awakens to and realizes that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding and indestructible;
however, because the depth and shallowness of the merit they thereby obtain are difficult to equalize, there is thus the "Chapter on the Differentiation of Merit.
Yet, the reason for this differentiation is not that our Buddha intentionally wished to divide it; rather, it arises from [the differences in] what has been attained.
The distinctions between these various realizations and their differences arise from the stages of attaining Buddhahood according to the number of kalpas spent in cultivation;

they are categorized thus because sentient beings have limited capacity for hearing, believing, and understanding the sutra. Up to this point constitutes the primary teaching of the Essential Gate (*honmon shōshū*);
all that follows belongs to the Propagation Gate (*ryūtsū*). As for what is compared in the final chapter mentioned above, it concerns those who have long practiced and attained actual realization.
This is a comparison. As for those who merely rejoice for a brief moment, how much more so would it be?
Furthermore, the World-Honored One stated that the merit of a single thought of rejoicing, transmitted successively down to the fiftieth person, exceeds that accumulated over eighty years.

If one were to extensively practice giving toward twelve skulls until all were led to realize the four fruits of the path, this would not equal even a ten-thousandth part of the merit of those who receive the Dharma, as it cannot be compared by means of calculation or metaphor. This clarifies the merits possessed by those who receive the Dharma;
however, regarding the Dharma masters who transmit the sutras, it is not so—they will certainly attain the purification of the six sense faculties.
Pure. One realizes all true marks (*dharmatā*). To discuss these comprehensively, the merits realized therein are entirely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

how could they be limited merely to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and the three insights (*trividyā*)? From the above comparison, one first sees that the merit of upholding this sutra is profound and firm.
Next, he further exhorts them to maintain it resolutely and never slacken even slightly, and further cites:
He constantly practiced the conduct of never disparaging others, transforming all sentient beings solely through the Buddha’s wisdom of equality.
Although he suffered much humiliation and insult, he never for a single moment felt weariness or resentment, until today he attained the fruit of Bodhi;
this too is a testament to the efficacy of upholding this sutra. Since the Tathāgata has already evaluated his merit and demonstrated his practice, and the assembled multitude has likewise...

Believing in its reality and understanding its purport, at that moment the World-Honored One—like a person burdened by layers of weight who has been released from their bonds, his entire body filled with joy and relief—immediately manifested great supernormal powers.
He extended his broad and long tongue; with a single cough and a snap of his fingers, his voice reached throughout the Sahā world.
With the light from a single pore of his body and the light from the mark of his tongue, he illuminated the emanations of the jewel trees. As...

In a single month, he appeared before the myriad waters; through the sound of the earth quaking in the ten directions and the voices of the holy and the ordinary, he manifested the wondrous events of this Sahā world, like a frost-bell emerging from a heavy siege. How could such supernatural powers be easily measured?
This is why it is called the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers. As for the "Chapter on Entrustment," it concerns the entrustment of all that has been previously taught and demonstrated.

This causes one to purify oneself and practice with utmost sincerity. From the chapter "Distinguishing Merits" up to this sixth chapter, it constitutes the ultimate point of wondrous realization, thereby exhausting the depths of awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

The subsequent six chapters collectively constitute the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and the circulation of that matter. The "Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja" exhorts [the practitioner] through ascetic practices.

The masters who propagate the sutra manifest wondrous sounds as they come and go, responding to the call and encouraging their disciples to uphold the Dharma. Avalokiteśvara enters the Universal Gate to manifest his presence;
seeing those who flow against the current, he drives his chariot in reverse. The assembly of sages employs divine mantras for empowerment, mobilizing a compassion that knows no limit.
King Miaozhuangyan comes forth to recount his past deeds, revealing the profound power of the Dharma—how could the transformation of consciousness be otherwise?
Difficult indeed. The Universal Sage is revered; his new exhortations to illuminate the path and benefit sentient beings are urgent, yet the future is inexhaustible.
Thereupon, the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas sing in unison the melody of non-arising: "I and all people shall join hands and ascend to the field of non-extinction.
At this moment, both this Dharma and these flowers are equally illusory; there is neither arising nor Buddha.
No-mind. *Tu!* Can it be called "entanglement"?

Regarding the five characters of the title of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra Xuanshou Hongchuan Xu* (The Preface to the Propagation of the Handing-Down of the Lotus Sutra), the explanation of the title has already been provided. As for the "Preface to the Propagation": "Hong" (弘) means vast and great; "Chuan" (傳) means to transmit.
It is a transmission. According to the original preface, that which praises [the teachings] beyond limit is called "extensive" (弘);

that which is handed down forever to future sages is called "transmission" (傳). A "preface" (序) means sequential order; it is like observing the eastern and western walls of a building, through which one can distinguish the depth and shallowness of the halls and rooms.
It is also a "thread-end" (頭緒); just as a thread gains its thread-end, its systematic organization comes into being. Thus, the Sūtras have prefaces.
This preface clarifies the general outline of the sutra and distinguishes its beginning from its end, ensuring that the underlying intent remains coherent and that each section has a clear standard.
Following this description of the title, the author next describes the person who composed the preface.
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Daoxuan of Zhongnan Mountain during the Tang Dynasty.
"Tang" indicates the era in which this preface was written. "Zhongnan Mountain" is named for its location eighty *li* south of the city of Chang'an, situated in Wugong County of Fufeng.
To the east it adjoins Mount Li and Mount Taibai; to the west it connects with Mount Taibai and Mount Long. As for that mountain:
Coming from the north, its influence culminates in the south; hence it is called Zhongnan (Culmination of the South).
It is also known as Zhongnan (Central South), for it lies in the center of heaven and to the south of the capital. It is also named Dili (Earth’s Lungs), as it can provide refuge from floods.

"Śramaṇa" is a general term for the sons of Śākya. In Sanskrit, *śramaṇa* means "diligent and tranquilizing": it signifies diligently cultivating all forms of goodness and extinguishing all evil deeds.
Furthermore, because he has stilled his mind and reached the fundamental source, he is titled a śramaṇa. "Upper Way, Lower Proclamation" (Shangdao Xiexuan) is the preface to the master’s name.
Because later students do not dare to refer to him by his name alone, it is called "Upper-Lower. The Master’s surname was Jian; he was a descendant of Pengzu.
He was a native of Changcheng County in Huzhou. His father was Jianshen, who served as the Minister of Personnel during the Sui dynasty.
His mother dreamed that a lunar disc pierced her womb before she conceived. She further dreamed of a Buddhist monk who said, "The one you carry in your womb is the Venerable You of the Liang dynasty.
He was born during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. Upon reaching maturity, he took ordination under Master Ying of Riyen Monastery at the age of [blank] years.

Tenth: He shaved his head and received full ordination, becoming profoundly versed in the Vinaya scriptures. In the seventh year of the Wude era (Jia-shen) of Emperor Gaozu of the Tang dynasty, he moved his residence to Zhuma Aranya on Mount Zhongnan and composed the *Xingshichao* (Commentary on Practice).
He once practiced the *Banzhou Sanmei* (Pratyutpanna Samādhi), during which there were twenty sessions in total;

Now, the term "as for" (*fúyǐ*) is a particle used to introduce a statement. What was previously called "descending as a spirit" (*jiànglíng*) refers collectively to all Buddhas;

how could this have been without cause? It was solely for the sake of all sentient beings who live drunk and die dreaming, their Buddha-eye unopened.
Were it not for the Greatly Awakened Sage, there would be no means to open up the vast teaching and transformation so as to lead them [to awakening].
