the subsequent equal bestowal of great vehicles is a metaphor for the current teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Although it consists of a mere few thousand words, there is nothing that exceeds this text in its thorough elucidation of how those of the Two Vehicles may enter the Great Vehicle; they follow one and the same track. This is its function.

The Record states: "Today, beneath Heaven, the carriage ruts are uniform, the written characters are uniform, and the conduct of the people is uniform. This refers to the refinement [of the teachings].

In terms of the principles of the Dharma, they are identical to the text of the single reality of the Perfect Teaching; in terms of metaphors, they are identical to the ruts of the single vehicle of the Great Chariot.
The phantom city preserves the traces of past conditions so that they do not fall into oblivion.
After the Tathāgata had bestowed predictions upon the five hundred disciples, he further explained the causal origins.
In one section, he cited how the Buddha himself, during the time of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Buddha, was a prince who preached the Lotus Sutra. At that time, those whom he transformed were constant...
The sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are none other than you, bhikṣus, and my śrāvaka disciples after my parinirvāṇa.
Thus, one should know that those who have received the prediction today possess causal conditions from former lives that have not been lost or discarded.
Therefore, the parable of the conjured city is taught.
The "Tying of the Jewel" illustrates that the nature of reality is ever-present.

The five hundred disciples, having understood the causes and conditions taught by the Buddha, received the prediction of their future fruition. Moved by the Buddha’s kindness and virtue, they spoke the parable of tying the jewel.
In this parable, the Buddha is likened to a close friend, while themselves are likened to intoxicated men; the One Vehicle—the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—is likened to the nature of reality.
The Jewel. Now, following the three cycles of teaching, each has attained awakening; it is like realizing after sobering from wine that the jewel one once possessed can now be used.
Although the Wisdom Buddha and the present Buddha have emerged from kalpas as numerous as dust motes, this jewel of the rational nature has never been lost;
therefore, it is said to be "ever-present."
The metaphor of digging a well illustrates the manifold methods for awakening.

This also follows from the preceding text. It means that although the pearl of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—the principle of nature—exists, if it were not for the Tathāgata revealing these manifold methods in this sutra, one would still be unable to experience its manifestation before oneself. Therefore, the Buddha...
In the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," he again exhorted them four times to diligently read, recite, receive, and uphold this sutra.
He spoke the parable of digging a well, stating that whether laypeople or monastics seeking the Buddha-way, if they practice according to other sutras, it is like seeking water on a high plateau;
one sees only dry earth, and though much effort is spent in digging, one is still far from reaching the water. If, however, one relies on this...

Through sustained cultivation—just as when one exerts effort without ceasing and gradually encounters moist soil until finally reaching mud, thereby knowing that water must be near—one understands that these scriptures elucidate the Tathāgata’s wondrous meaning of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
All of these are the Tathāgata’s instructions intended to lead beings to awakening through manifold skillful means (*upāya*).
Therefore, it is said: "He displays the various methods for awakening. (The character *záo* [pronounced *zuò*] refers to digging.)
The words and meanings are indeed as clear as if they were being explained face-to-face;
that is to say, from the "Introductory Chapter" to the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," although the words and meanings of the three cycles [of teachings] are said to be perfectly clear and manifest.
These points are repeatedly illustrated through various metaphors; when one contemplates their underlying intent, its meaning is exceedingly profound and vast.

When viewed from the perspective of words and literal meaning, they appear to be the common parlance of worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); yet, when considered in terms of their metaphorical intent, they actually clarify the supreme Great Meaning (*mahārtha*).
Thus far, the sūtra has been extolled to demonstrate the excellence of the Dharma it expounds. Hereafter, [the text] shall further extol its...
The Buddha, whose mind is capable of eloquent exposition, is wondrous;

were it not for his great compassion that universally rescues those mired in the stagnant currents of delusion, and his singular heart of pity that saves those who have lost their true nature in the darkness of ignorance.
It is said that although the phrasing and principles of this sutra are modeled with perfect fidelity, its parables and expositions are vast and profound in their intent.

Were it not for the Great Compassion and Universal Salvation of our Śākyamuni, who else could have drawn forth those śrāvakas who were stalled in emptiness or mired in mere traces, and those streams of people submerged in expedient views? Were it not for our Tathāgata...

With such supreme compassion, who else could rescue and receive those sentient beings who are ignorant, stubborn, and deluded, as well as those people who have lost their true nature due to ignorance?

Truly, observe how earnest his compassionate heart is; there are words that fall among the weeds, intended to conclude that were it not for a Great Sage, there would be no way to bring about transformation and enlightenment.
From the Han to the Tang dynasties, spanning over six hundred years, among more than four thousand fascicles of various scriptures that have been received and upheld,
none surpasses this sūtra in its prevalence.
From the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Han to the second year of the Qianfeng era of Emperor Gaozong of the Tang, the Vinaya masters entered...
It has been extinguished. Yet, it remains uncertain in which year of the Tang dynasty the preface was composed. A total of over six hundred years has passed; this is the length of time.
Having surveyed all the various texts—comprising the Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras—there are more than four thousand fascicles; this is the abundance of the Dharma.

Yet, that among the most extensive scriptures throughout the long course of time, people have singularly upheld this sūtra with such abundance and devotion serves as proof of the great compassionate heart of the Buddha’s empowerment; it also verifies the perfect resonance between the capacities of beings and the teachings;
and it demonstrates that the principles venerated in this era are not erroneous. Thus ends the praise of its propagation.

The exposition on the Buddha and the Dharma is concluded. Next, he further extols the Sangha. This is because the faculties [of the disciples] and the teachings are in accord; it is the marvel of hearing [the teaching] and deeply revering it.

Is this not the case where the faculties and the teachings strike one another, as in the "Residual Dust of Superior Wisdom" (Zhisheng-yi chen) heard by King Wensheng? Hearing this, one deeply reveres it, possessing the majesty of King Wen.
The remaining achievements also refer to those who, following the aforementioned, uphold [the teaching] with vigor. "Kou" (扣) means to strike, to cast oneself down, or to join together.

This refers to when the Buddha was in the world and personally preached this sutra; even then, there were many who felt resentment and jealousy, and as many as five thousand people withdrew from their seats. Now that the Buddha has passed into extinction...

After a long time, those who uphold [this teaching] have instead returned to such flourishing prosperity; is this not the convergence of capacity and teaching, and the union of sentient beings with the Buddha?

One must know that these instances of the mutual convergence of capacity and teaching are all the lingering traces left behind by the great seeds sown during the time when their wisdom surpassed that of the Buddha.
As the "Rhapsody on the Capital of Wei" states: "The mulberry and catalpa trees of the former kings stand in rows..."
The lingering dust of the Sage serves to moisten and refine one's writings. Those who hear this and feel deep reverence may be said to have found their faculties meeting with the teaching;

those who, upon hearing this sutra for the first time, immediately give rise to profound veneration, likewise possess the remaining merit of having once received a prediction of enlightenment from the Buddha Vimalacitra during the time of the Buddha Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja. This is due to the efficacy of past deeds. From these traces, the principle can be seen.
Today, there is a karmic affinity for this sutra. Those who hear it and respond with reverent faith should rejoice within themselves. This is the formal conclusion;
were it not for past affinities, there would be no means to guide the mind. (Ji, pronounced "ji")

I have therefore composed this preface at the beginning of each scripture to synthesize its essence, hoping thereby to purify the six sense organs early on, to look up to the auspicious assembly of the Compassionate Honored One,
to swiftly accomplish the four virtues, and to advance toward the profound path of the Land of Bliss.

"Zhué" means "exclusive. "Zōng" refers to the shuttle that holds the threads and regulates the warp. Regarding the purification of the six sense faculties, it is as explained in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master.

I have interwoven these explanations from the beginning of the sutra to compose this preface, so that people may understand the great purport of this scripture and cause those who receive and uphold it to apply themselves with single-minded devotion to their practice, thereby hopefully attaining early purification.

These are the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Looking up to the Compassionate Honored One, one considers that since Śākyamuni has already entered *parinirvāṇa*, if one wishes to enter the auspicious assembly of the Buddha, one must wait for Maitreya, the Compassionate Honored One, to preach the Dharma at the Dragon Flower Tree. If the six sense faculties are purified early on, one may look forward to that future auspicious assembly.
Regarding the swift accomplishment of the four virtues, it is said they are permanence, bliss, self, and purity (*nitya-sukha-ātman-śubha*); however—
These four kinds are the virtues of the fruit of Buddhahood. According to the *Samantabhadra-uddesa*, it says:
"If good men or women, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, wish to obtain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Buddha said:
'They should accomplish four dharmas: first, being protected and remembered by all Buddhas; second, planting the roots of all virtues; third, entering into right concentration.'"
The fourth is to give rise to the mind that seeks to rescue all sentient beings. Regarding the preface’s mention of "swift accomplishment," this is said in contrast to gradual purification;

it refers to the urgent task to be achieved within the causal stage. This means that if these four virtues are accomplished, they constitute the profound Great Way for proceeding toward the Land of Bliss.
"Yòu" (猷) is synonymous with "dào" (道). "Lètǔ" (樂土, Land of Bliss) follows the original text.

The Sūtra refers to the three transformations of the pure land. If one purifies the six sense faculties and looks up to Maitreya, the Compassionate Honored One, one will achieve the four virtues and may proceed to the Lotus Land of Ultimate Bliss.
How much more so when one’s practice is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled—one should enter the Pure Land of Mind-Only.
This very Sūtra also states: "If one practices as taught, after the end of life, one will immediately go to the World of Peace and Bliss."
[The text] concludes with the Great Bodhisattva Amitābha Buddha. Furthermore, this sutra places Maitreya at its beginning and Samantabhadra at its end;
by citing these two, one may encompass the entirety of the sutra from beginning to end. Kumārajīva has thus completed the first major section on the teaching of the One Great Time.
Fourth, he now summarizes the intent behind the wide propagation [of the text]. (The character *zhé* is pronounced *shè*; *zōng* is in the departing tone.)
"May its broad promotion be inexhaustible, forever bequeathed to posterity"—thus it concludes the title of the preface.
"Promotion" (*zàn*) means to assist; "bequeathed" (*yí*) means to transmit or to leave behind. The author of the preface states that he has composed this preface;
though his person is humble and his words light, they are like a handful of soil assisting Mount Tai or a ladle of water benefiting the vast ocean.
It is impossible to exhaustively describe even a ten-thousandth part of the merit of this sutra.

My sole wish is that by means of this preface, this sutra may be perpetuated for future generations and its circulation remain inexhaustible, merely to manifest my humble sincerity in a single thought of protecting the Dharma.
The phrase "yún'ěr" (thus it is said) is a concluding expression, meaning that the contents of the preface are exactly as stated herein. However—
This sutra possesses both the "trace" (jiji) and "origin" (honji) gates. Why, then, does this preface now only introduce the three assemblies of the trace gate?

Furthermore, the trace is manifested by means of the origin, and the origin is revealed through the trace. If one knows that the trace is bestowed from the origin, one simultaneously knows that the origin is revealed by means of the trace.
That is to say, although the origin and the trace differ, their inconceivable nature is one. Having thus completed the explanation of Master Kumārajīva’s preface, I transmit [this].
(Yin Yi). Preface to the Transmission of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* with the Hand Extended (End).
